res.verdict:
Hypothesis 5 is NOT supported. Neither test finds edge-on rings.

(1) Pair separation. Across all 2.16 M detected dots (1.50 M usable centres, shift null of 200-350 Å), the pair-correlation curve g(r) is flat at about 1.02 from 70 to 160 Å. There is no narrow excess at 85-110 Å: the window minus its flanks is -0.001 [-0.004, +0.002]. Thin, middle and thick ice look the same. The upper limit on a narrow excess is about 1.9k pairs in the whole data set. The rod-stream dot_pair_thread classes alone hold 21.4k unique detected pairs at 85-110 Å, so real pairs can explain at most about 9% of them. The anchor dot_pair classes, which show no thread at all, hold 68.6k pairs in the same window. A sharp dot pair at about 90 Å is what 2D classification makes from chance neighbours in this crowded ice. The anchor-stream dot_pair_thread classes have their two dots only 42-73 Å apart (median 58 Å), and around their A dots the 85-110 Å range is depleted (g = 0.82). They are short dumbbells, not ~106 Å rings.

(2) Thread density. In the rod-stream dot_pair_thread classes the middle of the A-B segment carries 0.25-0.47x a single duplex per Å (strip vs rod_no_dot; 186 = 0.30, 101 = 0.25), or 0.29-0.64x by the polar measure (vs dot_long_rod). An edge-on ring predicts at least 2x. The anchor-stream classes give 0.51-0.81x, but those segments are only 9-26 Å long and dominated by the tails of the two dots. The 34 Å repeat test could not decide anything (see caveats). The faint thread is less than one duplex, which fits occasional overlapping or blurred DNA, not two superposed strands.
res.key_numbers:
g_all at 85-110 Å = 1.017 [1.015, 1.020]; flanks (60-85 and 110-135 Å) = 1.018; bump = -0.001 [-0.004, +0.002]. Broad excess in the window = 14.8k pairs [12.5k, 17.1k] against 857k chance pairs, about 2% and flat across r, so it is not narrow. Upper limit on a narrow excess = 1.86k pairs.

Rod-stream dot_pair_thread pairs: 21,439 at 85-110 Å vs 3,593 under the rotation null. B dot matched in 41% of particles vs 8.3% null. Median separation 89.7 Å (p10-p90 81-102).
Anchor dot_pair (no thread): 68,578 pairs in the window.
Anchor dot_pair_thread: median separation 58 Å; 132 pairs in the window.

Thread / duplex: rod-stream classes 186 0.30, 101 0.25, 187 0.42, 188 0.43, 196 0.47 (strip); polar 0.29-0.64. Anchor classes 5 0.71, 19 0.51, 101 0.70; classes 33 and 59 have no measurable middle.

Same pose/shift convention for both streams (rot-th_shift-_particleframe). A dot hit at the mapped position: rods 0.86, anchors 0.74, vs 0.42 and 0.30 at a random angle.
caveats: The pair test only sees a far-rim 'dot' if the LoG detector picks it up (threshold 4.5 MAD). An edge-on rim too faint to detect would not appear in g(r). The class-average thread density (0.25-0.47x a duplex, against 2x predicted) covers that case independently.

The 34 Å repeat test could not decide anything. My on-axis periodogram at 5.68 Å/px shows no 34 Å peak even for the rod_no_dot duplex reference, whose best periods are scattered from 20 to 69 Å, and the thread middles are only 9-43 Å long. Class 196's 0.23 amplitude at 32 Å comes from a single bump over about 40 Å (n=956) and means nothing.

The anchor stream has no rod_no_dot class, so its duplex reference is the anchor dot_short_rod averages. These are heterogeneous (polar reference p10-p90 = 10.5-50.9), so the anchor-stream ratios are rough. Their short middles also include the tails of the two dots, which pushes the ratios up.

Thread density comes from CryoSPARC class averages. It assumes one intensity scale across classes within a job, and it is lowered if the B partner is spread outside the ±15-25 Å strip or the ±25° sector. The polar measure, matched to dot_long_rod at the same radii, partly corrects for this and gives at most 0.64x.

The first run used a 150-300 Å shift null. That let the source dot fall inside the 150-160 Å null annuli, which made g read 0.89 there. Integer dot coordinates also gave a ±1.5% sawtooth from bin to bin. The final run uses a 200-350 Å shift and a seeded ±0.5 px de-quantisation jitter, and all reported numbers come from it. The remaining ~2% broad offset of g above 1 is probably density structure on scales the shift null does not match. It is flat in r, so it does not affect the narrow-window test.

The dot-pair-at-85-110 Å selection in the dot_pair_thread classes comes from 2D classification. Their class-conditional g peaks (rod-stream 186: 1.15 at 85-110 Å) say nothing about rings unless the whole population shows an excess, and it does not.

The light class-average density check ran on the login node for a few seconds. The full analysis ran as Slurm jobs 60569245 (superseded) and 60570675 on the test partition, 8 CPUs, no GPU, about 4.5 min each. Nothing committed.

problems: Every number quoted in the report matches results/A5_edge_on.json and the intermediate npz. This includes g_window 1.017 [1.015, 1.020], flanks 1.018, bump -0.001 [-0.004, +0.002], the 1,858-pair narrow upper limit, 14.8k [12.5k, 17.1k] broad excess, 857k null pairs, rod dpt 21,439 vs 3,593 rotation null, B match 41% vs 8.3%, median 89.7 A (p10-p90 80.5-101.8), anchor dot_pair 68,578, anchor dpt median 58 A with 132 pairs, the thread ratios, and the convention hit rates 0.86/0.74 vs 0.42/0.30.

The 'at most ~9% of rod dpt pairs' bound only holds if ring pairs would form a narrow excess inside 85-110 A. An edge-on ring with sfGFP anywhere on its rim projects sfGFP-to-far-end distances between R and 2R, about 53-106 A plus linker, so the excess could be broad and partly in the 60-85 / 110-135 flanks. I re-derived the bound against a ring-free baseline (mean g over 135-160 A = 1.021) with a 300x micrograph bootstrap. Excess pairs are -2.9k [-5.6k, 0] at 85-110 A, -0.6k [-6.6k, +5.0k] at 75-135 A and +2.1k [-1.1k, +5.6k] at 100-130 A. The robust upper limit is therefore about 5-5.6k pairs, which is up to ~25% of the 21.4k rod dpt window pairs, not 9%. That is still far below what the hypothesis needs.

The thread test uses class averages, so it measures a population mean. A mean of 0.25-0.47x a duplex (strip), or 0.29-0.64x (polar), excludes these classes being mostly edge-on rings. It does not exclude a minority: if the rest contribute nothing, up to ~12-24% (strip) or ~15-32% (polar) of the class particles could be ideal 2x edge-on rings. For the rod-stream dpt classes (83,928 particles, 87% A-mapped) that is roughly 10-20k particles. If far rims fall below the LoG detection threshold, this is the only bound, and the report's 'Neither test finds edge-on rings' / 'not two superposed strands' wording overstates it.

Dismissing the anchor dpt classes as 'too short for a ~106 A ring' is geometrically incomplete. With sfGFP part-way along an edge-on bar, the sfGFP-to-end distance runs from about 53 to 106 A and piles up near 53 A. My read-only line profiles through the class averages show no density beyond A on the side opposite B (s = -40 to -90 A is at or below background in anchors 5, 19, 33, 59 and 101). So there is no second bar end, and with thread <1x the conclusion still holds, but on that evidence rather than on length alone.

'Thin, middle and thick ice look the same' is true only for 70-160 A (window-minus-flank bump +0.002 / -0.012 / 0.000). At short range the terciles differ strongly (g in the 40-45 A bin = 1.07 / 1.54 / 1.32).

Possible defocus confound checked: defocus does not covary with relative ice thickness (Spearman -0.03). Splitting g_all by defocus tercile gives no window excess (window minus flanks -0.001 / -0.004 / +0.002; window minus 135-160 baseline -0.009 / -0.006 / +0.003). The 3x3 defocus x ice cells scatter ±0.02 with no consistent positive sign. The short-range excess (45-60 A, about 8.6k [6.2k, 11.0k] pairs above baseline) grows with defocus (42 A bin 1.08 -> 1.18 -> 1.27), which points to a CTF/detector artefact, not structure. The report does not mention this short-range excess.

A selection effect the report misses, which supports its conclusion: rod dpt classes 186 and 101 are strongly enriched in the thinnest-ice tercile (55% and 58%, against 21% for rod_no_dot and 28% for dot_long_rod), and so is anchor dot_pair (42%). Thin ice carries the highest dot density (Spearman of ice vs eligible centres per micrograph = -0.62). That fits chance pairs from crowding, and argues against upright ~110 A rings, which would favour thicker ice.

Class-based pair geometry is clipped by the 2D circular mask: class-average density is exactly 0 beyond about 120-130 A from the box centre, and two_dots limits the B search to rr < 115 A. Class B partners beyond ~110-115 A cannot be found. The global g(r) from micrograph coordinates is not affected.

Minor: g_all is about 1.000-1.002 at 65-75 A and 1.015-1.026 from 75 to 160 A, so 'flat at ~1.02 from 70 A' is slightly loose. The rods random-angle convention control (0.42) is weak because A sits only ~12 A from the box centre, but B matching at 41% vs 8.3% under rotation independently confirms the mapping at ~90 A.

Process: scripts/43_A5_edge_on_ring_test.py already exists in HEAD (commit 91fa835), and this run changed the tracked file in the working tree (shift null 150-300 -> 200-350 A, jitter, add_verdict). It is not a new untracked file, so this conflicts with 'do not modify existing scripts' unless 43 counts as this task's own file.
v.corrected_statement: Hypothesis 5 (intact rings lying edge-on, filed as dot_pair_thread classes) is not supported, and the data do not need it. Across 1.50 M eligible dot centres (2.16 M detected dots), the shift-null pair correlation is about 1.015-1.026 from 75 to 160 A. There is no excess at 85-110 A, either against the flanks (window minus flanks -0.001 [-0.004, +0.002]; at most ~1.9k pairs) or against a ring-free 135-160 A baseline (-2.9k [-5.6k, 0] pairs). A ring signal spread over 75-135 A is limited to at most about 5-5.6k pairs. That is at most ~25% (about 9% if the signal is narrow) of the 21.4k detected 85-110 A pairs in the rod-stream dot_pair_thread classes, and far fewer than the 68.6k such pairs in the anchor dot_pair classes, which show no thread at all. The window result is the same in every ice and defocus tercile; defocus barely covaries with ice. The rod dpt classes are concentrated in the thinnest, most crowded ice (55-58% vs 21% for rod_no_dot), which fits chance neighbour pairs selected by 2D classification. In the class averages, the middle of the A-B segment carries 0.25-0.47x a single duplex per A (strip vs rod_no_dot), or 0.29-0.64x (polar vs dot_long_rod), against at least 2x predicted for an edge-on ring. So these classes are not mostly rings. Because a class average is a population mean, though, a minority of up to ~12-32% edge-on rings with an undetectable far rim cannot be excluded. The anchor dot_pair_thread classes are 42-73 A dumbbells with a sub-duplex link and no density beyond A on the side opposite B, so they do not show the projection of an edge-on ring. The 34 A repeat readout cannot discriminate at 5.68 A/px. Separately, the short-range pair excess at 45-60 A grows with defocus, which suggests a detector/CTF artefact and should be followed up.

res.verdict: Hypothesis 4 (rings survive in thick ice) is not supported. The thickest tertile shows no ring-like average, no extra dots at the DNA ends that 2D classification did not select on, and no longer attached DNA. The label census does shift with ice thickness, but most of that shift tracks crowding: thin ice holds about 1.8x more detected dots. A small dot_long_rod excess (+4.7 points) remains after matching on dot density, but rod_no_dot rises too (+3.7). Among rod classes, the dot-bearing share actually falls in thick ice (62% to 52%), the opposite of what H4 predicts. Hole test (scripts/41 describe, imported unmodified): no strict hole in any class, stratum or stream (72 rod and 88 anchor classes have at least 300 particles in every tertile). Three lenient hits (z>1.5 mask, hole at least 20 A) are 23-32 A gaps in noise_junk or ice_contaminant classes (rods 53 and 181, anchors 31), not 50-70 A ring holes. Per-tertile averages look like the CryoSPARC ones (median r = 0.79 for rods, 0.87 for anchors, so the pose convention is right).
res.key_numbers:
Ice tertiles (n = 2679/2678/2679 micrographs; cuts 1.0693 and 1.0804; top decile at least 1.0883). Ice vs CTF fit resolution rho +0.64, vs dot density -0.68, vs defocus -0.03, vs acquisition time +0.19. About 61% of the ice variance is between foil holes.
Dots/um^2, T1 to T3: 5153 to 2873.
Rods stream, T1 to T3: dot_long_rod 22.3% to 28.1%; rod_no_dot 12.5% to 23.4%; dot_pair_thread 24.5% to 8.0%.
Anchors stream: dot_pair 74.7% to 50.5%; dot_short_rod 6.7% to 17.5%.
After matching on dot density, T3 minus T1: dot_long_rod +4.7 points [3.8, 5.4]; rod_no_dot +3.7; dot_pair_thread -4.6.
dot_long_rod 2h: 78.0 to 76.6 A (window-limited, class mix).
Dots within 35 A of a rod end, obs/shift null: on selection-light ends (rod_no_dot ends plus far ends of dot classes) 0.65 / 0.76 / 0.78 / 0.78 (top decile); excess per dot -0.0038 to -0.0034. Density-matched T3 minus T1 ratio -0.001 [-0.046, 0.044]. The selected near end reads 6.5 to 10.7x, but its excess per um^2 is flat (171 vs 172), so the rise is a lower chance baseline, not more attachment.
caveats: ice_thickness_rel covers a narrow range (most micrographs 1.05-1.10) and tracks CTF fit quality (rho 0.64). The thick tertile is also worse-fit and collected later, so the test has limited leverage. Thicker ice also does not guarantee particles stay off the air-water interface.

Dot detection uses a per-micrograph threshold, so the lower detected dot density in thick ice can be partly an SNR effect, not a lower real concentration. Both chance coincidences and the 2D label mix scale with crowding. Only the density-matched contrasts and the OLS fits with dot density as a covariate partly control for this.

Even the selection-light ends sit below chance (0.65-0.78) in every tertile. This repeats the 2D-window depletion flagged in rod_end_coloc_review.json, so the end-dot proxy is biased, and only its change between tertiles is read here. The anchors density-matched contrast used only one density bin (anchors exist on just 2,009 micrographs), so it is weak.

Per-tertile averages reuse the pooled round-1 2D poses and classes. A rare ring subpopulation hidden inside a large class, or never pulled into its own class, would be diluted and could still be missed. No synthetic positive control for the hole detector was run, per the no-synthetic-particles rule.

The test-partition QOS allows 5 jobs per user, so the job arrays were replaced by single multi-CPU jobs. All runs were CPU-only on the test partition. Nothing was committed, and no existing scripts were modified (scripts 17 and 41 are imported unmodified).

problems: Every headline number in the report matches results/A7_ice_tertiles.json and permic.csv.gz. That covers the tertile sizes and cuts (1.0693/1.0804/p90 1.0883), the correlations (rho 0.64 with CTF fit, -0.68 with dot density, -0.03 with defocus, +0.19 with time), the 61% between-hole variance, dot densities 5153 to 2873, the label fractions for both streams, the density-matched contrasts (+4.7 [3.8, 5.4], +3.7, -4.6, -0.001 [-0.046, 0.044]), dot_long_rod 2h 78.0 to 76.6, the light-end ratios 0.65/0.76/0.78/0.78, the near end 6.5 to 10.7x with 171 vs 172 per um^2, and the lenient hole hits (rods 53 and 181, anchors 31). The problems below are about interpretation, not arithmetic.

The verdict says the dot-bearing share among rods falls in thick ice (62% to 52%), 'the opposite of what H4 predicts'. The 62% and 52% are frac_dot_long_rod_of_R: dot_long_rod over all rods in rods_analysed, with dot_short_rod left out of the numerator. When I matched on dot density (same deciles and weighting as the script), the share of dot classes among rod classes changed by only -0.3 points between T3 and T1. The fall is therefore explained by crowding (the chance near-end null per rod is about halved in thick ice) and is not evidence against H4. That sentence should be dropped.

'No longer attached DNA' was not actually tested. The rods_analysed h is a class-average geometry assigned to every particle: p90 is 86.7 A, no rod reaches 150 A, and the DNA is about 170 A. It can only show the class mix. The per-tertile average mask length that the script itself stores (averages.rods.summary.mask_length_A_weighted_by_label) does rise for dot_long_rod: 83.1, 85.8, 89.7 A from T1 to T3. Per class, 11 go up, 2 go down and 11 are unchanged (median change 0). rod_no_dot also rises by 3.4 A. The verdict leaves this out. It is small, SNR-sensitive and not specific to dot classes, but it points weakly in the H4 direction and should be reported. The statement should say that DNA length could not be measured, not that it was not longer.

Ice is confounded with shot position in the hole. Each foil hole has three EPU template positions. The third position (Data_12351290) reads thicker ice (1.084 vs 1.070), has 34% fewer detected dots, a worse CTF fit (4.5 vs 4.0 A) and more astigmatism (162 vs 144 A), whatever order it was shot in. 61% of third-position shots fall in T3 and only 6.6% in T1. Hole plus position explains 72% of the ice variance (about 11% from position alone). So T3 partly means 'position 3', which is possibly nearer the hole edge or at a larger image shift. When I recomputed tertiles within each position, positions 1 and 2 reproduce the trends, and the light-end excess per dot is flat at -0.0035 to -0.0038 everywhere. The conclusion survives, but this confound should be stated.

The pooled defocus rho of -0.03 hides structure inside foil holes: within a hole, ice correlates with defocus at r = -0.25 and with time at r = +0.49, because of shot order and position. 'Defocus does not covary' is true only between micrographs pooled across holes.

The per-tertile averages are blurrier than the CryoSPARC ones. Large rod classes measure about 110 A instead of about 130 A, and class 83 measures 47 A instead of 136 A. Several big classes correlate poorly with the CryoSPARC averages: 44 ice_contaminant r = 0.03 (74k particles), 186 dot_pair_thread r = 0.37 (57k), 105 dot_pair r = 0.21 (18k). A median r of 0.79 supports the pose convention overall, but the hole detector has lower sensitivity on these averages than on the CryoSPARC ones, and the caveat should say so.

On the selected near end, the excess per detected dot roughly doubles, from 0.034 in T1 to 0.062 in T3. After density matching it is still +0.009 and positive in all 9 density bins. Saying the excess per um^2 is flat (171 vs 172) is only one normalisation. Per detected sfGFP, slightly more dots sit at dot-class rod ends in thick ice. This is the selected end, and the denominator depends on SNR, so it is weak, but it points in the H4 direction and should be stated alongside the dot_long_rod residual (+4.7, offset by rod_no_dot +3.7).

Minor points. (1) The raw light-end ratio rises significantly with ice (+0.13 [0.11, 0.16]) and drops to zero only after density matching; the report handles this correctly. (2) The density matching is lopsided: most bins have very unequal T1/T3 counts (for example 52 vs 495), the top decile is dropped, and the anchors contrast uses one bin. (3) The script appears in a git commit (91fa835, the report.md commit); the uncommitted changes since then are cosmetic figure edits only.
v.corrected_statement: Hypothesis 4 (closed rings survive in thicker ice and open at the air-water interface) is not supported, but this test has little leverage. Across ice_thickness_rel tertiles (n = 2679/2678/2679; a narrow range of about 1.05-1.10), no per-tertile class average in either stream has a strict scripts/41 hole. The three lenient hits are 23-32 A gaps in noise_junk or ice_contaminant classes, not 50-70 A ring holes. The per-tertile averages are blurrier than the CryoSPARC ones (median r = 0.79 for rods, 0.87 for anchors), so a rare ring subpopulation inside pooled classes could still be missed. Dots within 35 A of the rod ends that 2D did not select on stay below chance in every tertile, and their excess per detected dot is flat (-0.0038 to -0.0034; density-matched T3 minus T1 ratio -0.001 [-0.046, 0.044]). This also holds when tertiles are defined within each shot position. The label census changes strongly with ice, but most of the change tracks crowding: thin ice has about 1.8x more detected dots. After matching on dot density, the share of dot-bearing classes among rod classes does not change (-0.3 points), so the raw drop from 62% to 52% does not count against H4. What remains is a small dot_long_rod excess in thick ice (+4.7 points [3.8, 5.4]), largely offset by more rod_no_dot (+3.7). Near-end dots per detected dot are also slightly higher (+0.009 after matching). Both are small and selection- or SNR-dependent, and neither is a clear sign of attachment. Attached DNA length could not really be measured. The rods_analysed 2h is a class-geometry, window-limited readout (about 77-78 A, never 150 A or more). The per-tertile average mask length for dot_long_rod rises from 83 to 90 A, but rod_no_dot also rises by 3 A and the median per-class change is 0. Ice thickness is confounded with CTF fit (rho 0.64), acquisition time, and above all the third shot position in each foil hole (thicker, fewer dots, worse fit, more astigmatism; 61% of those shots are in T3). Within foil holes it also covaries with defocus (r = -0.25). The test therefore finds no positive evidence for intact rings in thicker ice, but it cannot strongly exclude H4.
